implementation_notes: The .NET realization is cooperative cancellation plus a timed wait: a CancellationTokenSource created with a TimeSpan (or armed with CancelAfter) cancels its token when the countdown elapses, and the operation observes it only if it accepts the token; for APIs that cannot take a token, Task.WaitAsync(TimeSpan) returns a task that faults with TimeoutException when the budget expires. The countdown starts when CancelAfter is called and a later CancelAfter resets it, so a shared source is not a reusable deadline. There is no language-level timeout, and the token/timed-wait pair replaces the classic timer-and-cancel structure; the hand-written form is justified only when an operation exposes neither a token nor an awaitable task.
pitfalls: Task.WaitAsync(TimeSpan) stops only the wait: the underlying task keeps running and may still complete with side effects, so pass a cancellation token when the operation itself must stop.

A token cancelled by its own timer and a token cancelled by the caller raise the same OperationCanceledException; check IsCancellationRequested (or use a linked source) so a caller cancellation is not reported as a timeout.
CancellationTokenSource is IDisposable and CancelAfter allocates a timer: a per-call source that is not disposed leaks the registration.
CancelAfter(TimeSpan) throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException once the delay exceeds Int32.MaxValue milliseconds, so very long budgets need a different mechanism.
